SUBJECT BC-01 / UNION CROWN

Prime Secretary
Josiah Richards

Josiah Richards began his career in the Fast Stream in 1998 as a Higher Executive Officer (HEO). Over the following decades, he rose through the ranks of the Civil Service, building the influence that would eventually carry him to the centre of government. During the riots of 2024, he seized power. By 2025, he had become the Prime Secretary of the United Kingdom, a title that replaced Prime Minister. Now, his authority hangs over the abandoned halls of Brent Cross, where his image promises order and his presence inspires fear. Spectral Ability: Union Crown. His reach extends into every abandoned wing of Brent Cross.

ALIGNMENT: NEUTRAL EVIL
ORIGIN: NORWICH, EAST ANGLIA, UNITED KINGDOM
FACTION: PSRM

        THE SECRETARY IS DEAD

        AFTER THE SHADOW

        The long, oppressive shadow that had blanketed the British Isles finally lifted with the sudden and absolute downfall of the Prime Secretary. For nearly a decade, the telescreens of Whitehall had broadcast a singular, unyielding will, but tonight they flickered to black before resetting to a simple, quiet dial tone. In the streets of London, Edinburgh, Cardiff, and Belfast, the suffocating tension that had dictated daily life dissolved into an unfamiliar, breathless silence, followed quickly by the rising crescendo of collective relief.

        With the regime dismantled, the ancient halls of Parliament were reopened, stripped of the authoritarian banners that had defaced their stone walls. Peace, fragile but deeply yearned for, swept across the United Kingdom like a cool autumn breeze, mending the deep fractures left behind by years of strict rationing and surveillance. Neighbors who had long looked at one another with suspicion stepped across their thresholds, sharing stories and rekindling the communal spirit that tyranny had sought to extinguish.

        The rebuilding process began not with steel and concrete, but with the quiet restoration of truth and justice. Monuments dedicated to the Prime Secretary’s vanity were systematically dismantled, their stone repurposed to pave new public squares named after the brave dissidents who had kept the flame of liberty alive. Across the rolling hills of the countryside and the bustling avenues of the post-industrial north, a nation once forced into lockstep began to rediscover its diverse and vibrant identity.

        As the sun set on the first true year of liberation, the United Kingdom stood transformed, no longer an empire of fear but a sanctuary of renewed hope. The scars of the past remained, etched into the architecture and the memories of those who survived, serving as a permanent reminder of the cost of complacency. Yet, looking forward into the twilight, the people knew that the true strength of the realm lay not in the absolute power of a single ruler, but in the enduring resilience of its freedom.

        THE PRIME SECRETARY / RESISTANCE

        AFTER THE CHAINS

        Kevin Murderhorn was dead. His threat to destroy mankind ended in the atrium of Brent Cross, where the Resistance and Union Crown finally broke his hold.

        Peace returned to the United Kingdom. The fighting stopped, families came home, and the work of rebuilding began. Josiah Richards surrendered and was sent to prison to answer for his rule.

        Soon afterwards, he was pardoned in recognition of his decisive part in stopping the nihilistic terrorist. The pardon did not erase the suffering of his regime. It gave him a chance to live differently—and a responsibility to make that chance count.

        Beside Emma, Josiah faced a future without a throne. For once, protecting the world meant letting others choose its path.

        PROJECT BC / SIEGE OF BRENT CROSS
        AFTERMATH

        A COUNTRY STILL IN CHAINS

        The United Kingdom remained in turmoil. The guns at Brent Cross fell silent, but there were no crowds waiting to celebrate. Smoke drifted through the broken galleries. Beyond the police cordons, families searched lists of the missing, and ambulances carried away people whose names would never reach a parliamentary statement.

        Josiah Richards, Peter Chambers and Kevin Murderhorn were dead. Emma Richards had died in captivity. Their deaths brought an end to the siege, but they did not settle what the country had become. In Whitehall, offices reopened beneath fresh portraits. The checkpoints remained. So did the surveillance, the shortages and the fear of a knock after midnight.

        Elizabeth Sterling took office as Prime Minister and declared the Metaphysical Deficit. Its meaning remained uncertain; its consequences did not. Emergency orders arrived before any public explanation. Buildings were sealed. Records disappeared into restricted archives. Those who asked when normal government would return were told that the danger had not yet passed.

        The Resistance, once useful in the struggle against Josiah, was named a terrorist organisation. Serving and former civil servants found their photographs on wanted notices. Their accounts were frozen, their colleagues questioned, their families watched. Gareth Williams and Alissa Roberts had survived Brent Cross only to discover that the government they had helped make possible now demanded their surrender.

        There would be no return for Mariah Banu. Murderhorn had killed her, and with her death the promise of a restored government became another story people lowered their voices to tell. Across London, Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast, grief hardened into anger. Protests met cordons; cordons became curfews. Each new restriction was announced as the measure that would finally make the next one unnecessary.

        At Westminster, the green benches filled again. Cameras recorded orderly debates while an unfamiliar stillness gathered beneath the chamber. Sterling spoke of recovery, of duty, of the sacrifices required to preserve the nation. Behind her, for a moment too brief for the evening news, the light seemed to bend.

        The siege was over. The United Kingdom was not at peace. In the dark between one emergency broadcast and the next, people waited to learn what their survival would cost.

        THE END

        SIEGE OF BRENT CROSS
